The Mole-like rice tenrec Oryzorictes hova is a small, shrew-like afrotherian mammal endemic to the wetlands of Madagascar, where its life history traits reflect the constraints of an insectivorous diet in a seasonally unpredictable environment. One of the most striking physiological features of this species is its basal metabolic rate, which has been measured at ~68.7 milliliters per hour [JOi = 68.7 milliliters per hour] when individuals are resting under thermoneutral conditions at 30.9 °C [T = 30.9 °C]. This rate is relatively high for an afrotherian of its size, likely reflecting the energetic demands of maintaining a stable body temperature while foraging in cool, waterlogged soils. Neonates, which are altricial and entirely dependent on maternal care, weigh approximately 4 grams [Wwb = approximately 4 grams] at birth, a value estimated from the congener Microgale dobsoni due to the difficulty of capturing pregnant females in the wild. This low birth mass is consistent with the reproductive strategy of many tenrecids, which produce large litters of poorly developed young.

Reproduction in Oryzorictes hova is characterized by a remarkably slow pace, with females typically producing only a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], despite having a potential litter size of 1 to 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 4 pups per litter]. This low fecundity may be linked to the species' reliance on patchy invertebrate prey, which imposes limits on the energy that a lactating female can allocate to offspring production. Under the same stable thermal conditions recorded for the species' resting metabolism (30.9 °C [T = 30.9 °C]), the duration from fertilisation to parturition, or gestation time, has been estimated at 35 days [tg = 35 days], which is relatively short compared to other tenrecs of similar body mass. Following birth, the suckling juvenile remains dependent on its mother's milk for an extended period; weaning, defined as the cessation of lactation and the transition to solid food, occurs approximately 76 days after birth [tx = approximately 76 days after birth] at a temperature of 30.9 °C [T = 30.9 °C]. This lengthy pre-weaning phase likely facilitates the gradual development of the juvenile's thermoregulatory and foraging capabilities in the challenging montane environment.

Juveniles that successfully navigate the weaning transition enter a prolonged period of growth and somatic development before reaching reproductive maturity. Under the ambient temperature regime typical of the species' active period (30.9 °C [T = 30.9 °C]), the age at which puberty is attained is estimated at approximately 200 days after birth [tp = approximately 200 days after birth], a figure that aligns with the comparatively slow life-history pace observed in other small-bodied Tenrecidae. This delayed maturation likely reflects the substantial accumulation of body mass required before gonadal development can commence, as females must reach an ultimate wet weight of around 45 grams [Wwi = around 45 grams] to support successful gestation and lactation. Field surveys indicate that adult females typically range from 28 to 40 grams [Wwi = from 28 to 40 grams], suggesting that the 45 gram value may represent an upper limit attained only under exceptionally favorable resource conditions. The disparity between average and maximum adult mass highlights the sensitivity of this species to habitat quality and prey availability.

Longevity in Oryzorictes hova is poorly documented, but available data suggest that individuals may survive for up to 6 years [am = up to 6 years] under stable environmental conditions at 30.9 °C [T = 30.9 °C], though this estimate remains highly uncertain. This figure would be unusually high for a mammal of such small body mass, and it may reflect the protective benefits of a fossorial lifestyle against predation and extreme climatic events. The congeneric Microgale dobsoni, upon which the birth mass estimate is based, is known to exhibit similarly extended lifespans in captivity. The species' slow life-history strategy—characterized by low fecundity, delayed maturation, and potentially extended longevity—appears to be an adaptation to the unpredictable resource pulses of Madagascar's highland wetlands, where years of plenty may alternate with periods of severe food shortage. Mortality during such lean periods likely falls heavily on dispersing juveniles and post-reproductive adults.

The maximum daily reproductive rate for the Mole-like rice tenrec has been estimated at approximately 1 pup per year [Ri = approximately 1 pup per year] when integrated over the breeding cycle, reflecting the combination of small litter size and infrequent litters. A particularly unusual aspect of this species' life history is the pronounced asynchrony between the attainment of sexual maturity and the onset of actual breeding. Although females may reach puberty at around 200 days after birth [tp = around 200 days after birth] under the standard thermal conditions of 30.9 °C [T = 30.9 °C], first successful reproduction is often deferred until the following breeding season, resulting in an effective age at first parturition that may exceed one year. This delay likely arises from the need to accumulate sufficient body reserves—specifically, reaching the ultimate wet weight of approximately 45 grams [Wwi = approximately 45 grams]—before the energetic demands of gestation and lactation can be sustained. The combination of a modest neonatal mass of 4 grams [Wwb = 4 grams] and an adult mass of up to 45 grams [Wwi = up to 45 grams] suggests that growth is a protracted process, with juveniles requiring many months to traverse this tenfold body mass range. This life-history pattern, with its extended developmental phases and conservative reproductive output, contrasts markedly with the fast-paced life cycles typical of many mainland insectivorous mammals of comparable size.
